speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Hon. C. D. HOWE (Minister of Transport) :
speakerposition: Minister of Transport
subtopic: FIRE-BOAT PROTECTION FOR VANCOUVER WATERFRONT
speechtext: On Friday last the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Green) asked a question about the fire-boat Pluvius at Vancouver. This boat was built in Norway in 1904 for use as a whaler, and was purchased and brought to Vancouver in 1931 for use as a fire-boat. Her annual cost of operation has amounted to 831,500. As will be seen from the date of construction, the boat is very old. It was condemned by the marine department as unsatisfactory, and repairs were ordered which would cost in excess of 828.000 before a certificate of seaworthiness could be issued after December 31, 1936. The whole situation was considered'. It was found that the boat was totally inadequate for the service required. There had been two major fires in the harbour since the Pluvius was put in commission in 1931, and in neither case was this boat able to render the slightest service in checking the fire. The harbour commissioners therefore approached the city with the request that they join in considering some more efficient means of fighting fires in Vancouver harbour, and I understand the matter is still under consideration between them.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Hon. CHARLES A. DUNNING (Minister of Finance) moved the second reading of Bill No. 42, to amend the Old Age Pensions Act.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCLUDE CERTAIN CLASSES OF BLIND PERSONS
speechtext: Is the minister not going to speak now?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCLUDE CERTAIN CLASSES OF BLIND PERSONS
speechtext: I did not intend to say anything further on the motion for second reading beyond what I said on the introduction of the resolution. The principle of the bill, which is adopted at this stage, is I think unanimously concurred in by the house, being the granting of pensions to blind persons at the age of forty years. The detailed provisions can be much more easily considered in committee than on the motion for second reading, and I was hoping we might go right into committee, when I shall be prepared to deal with every phase of the matter.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCLUDE CERTAIN CLASSES OF BLIND PERSONS
speechtext:
I
should like to say something on the general principle of the bill-certainly not in criticism of the minister; rather I congratulate him upon bringing it down. There might be some possible criticism in committee as regards the provision relating to two blind people marrying, but that I realize is for the committee stage. And I know the minister will not allow us to open the act in so far as old age pensions generally are concerned. But there are phases of the situation, and the manner in which the Old Age Pensions Act is now being carried out, which could legitimately be debated now, because they will affect blind people, as they will be subject to the same conditions. Therefore I should like to draw attention briefly to two or three of them.
The act itself is the Old Age Pensions Act. There is little to find fault with in it except that I think we should all be glad if the government would allow the eligible age to be reduced say to sixty-five years; and there are some provisions as regards residence qualifications which we would like to see changed. I realize that it would be out of order to move an amendment of that kind to this bill. It is of the regulations made under this act, some of the conditions to which blind people will be subjected, that I wish more particularly to complain. I am free to confess, as far as I am concerned, that the objections and complaints are largely due to the manner in which the British Columbia government carry out their understanding of the regulations.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCLUDE CERTAIN CLASSES OF BLIND PERSONS
speechtext: Not under this act. My hon. friend is discussing British Columbia legislation.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCLUDE CERTAIN CLASSES OF BLIND PERSONS
speechtext:
Quite so. The Parents'
Maintenance Act of British Columbia contains a provision under which any body or any person can sue. I said to the pension board, which is under the control of the British Columbia government, " Give the old man or woman the pension to which he or she is entitled now. Then you go ahead and sue their children, whom you think should pay." There are very few cases in which there are children who are so unfeeling as to allow their old parents to accept the old age pensions if they can afford to support them.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCLUDE CERTAIN CLASSES OF BLIND PERSONS
speechtext: There are a great many in Canada.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCLUDE CERTAIN CLASSES OF BLIND PERSONS
speechtext: There are not a great many in British Columbia, but in such cases 1 believe the mere threat of the board to sue would be sufficient to compel these children to look after their parents. In many other cases, however, the slightest investigation would show that the children were unable to contribute anything. A son may have three or four children of his own, and be living on relief.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCLUDE CERTAIN CLASSES OF BLIND PERSONS
speechtext: And a man may have $40,000 or $50,000.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCLUDE CERTAIN CLASSES OF BLIND PERSONS
speechtext:
I would suggest that the old man or old woman be given the pension, and that the board should sue such children and expose them in public. That would be far better than saying to the old woman, " You go and sue your son." She has neither the desire from the human point of view nor the money to sue her children. I am only suggesting that this act should be administered in a different way, so to speak.
Then there is another petty ruling-I cannot say it is a regulation, because this is purely a demand by the British Columbia board- which is used as a pretext to refuse or delay applications. I just came across it the other day, and I only mention it because it is one of many such rulings. To try and. get an old age pension in British Columbia is like trying to get into the senate; it is just about as difficult and takes just about as long. Members of parliament have to do these things

Old Age Pensions-Mr. Neill
for nothing, and they involve a tremendous amount of work. In the case I have in mind an old couple had been in Saskatchewan for a number of years, having come from Nova Scotia originally. They had) gone to church in Nova Scotia and when they moved to Saskatchewan they met the same pastor there. Later they all came to British Columbia, and the old people came to the district which I represent. On their behalf I applied for an old age pension, and in British Columbia you must furnish an affidavit by someone who knew them for a certain period of years in the province where they previously lived. So I had this reverend gentleman, a minister of the gospel of high standing in Vancouver, sign an affidavit that he had known these people in Saskatchewan, and that they had been there for the required period of years. It took me some time to get that affidavit signed, and then it was returned to me by -the board in Vancouver with an intimation that it would not suffice, that I would have to get such an affidavit from someone now resident in Saskatchewan. This old couple bad been away from Saskatchewan for ten or fifteen years, and after the lapse of that space of time it was very difficult to find anyone who remembered! them during the period they were there. This reverend gentleman, this man of God, of good repute, well known in Vancouver, swore that he had known them in Saskatchewan for a number of years, but that was not sufficient. Heaven only knows why:	this
could have been checked up very easily, since ' this gentleman lived only a few blocks from the board's offices in Vancouver, but his affidavit was not sufficient, so we had to dig up somebody in Saskatchewan, which was very difficult.
I do not see that public funds are guaranteed or made safer in this manner. Apparently these regulations are designed to make as much trouble as possible. Since I am on the subject, I remember taking up some cases with Hon. Mr. Gordon, when he was Minister of Labour. I named half a dozen cases in British Columbia, and he undertook to investigate them. I remember one particularly bad case. The answer that came to him was, "We have no evidence in this office that this woman is even seventy years of age." I had been citing her case in this house, and had said that this woman had been unfairly treated and discriminated against. They came back with the retort, "Why, Mr. Neill has not even proved that the woman is over seventy years of age," which, of course, is an elementary qualification. Mr. Gordon naturally put that up to me, and what was my -explanation? She had put in her application an-d had sent in 
her birth certificate. Her application was refused, and they sent the certificate back to her, accompanied by a letter saying that they noted that she was over seventy years of age. But when the minister took up the case they were technically correct in saying there was no evidence in that office as to her age, because they had sent the certificate back to her. That was deemed sufficient answer to my complaint. I can give the minister particulars about it, if it will do good-.
Then, I have here the form-it is an elaborate one-setting out some of the information required; it is not required by regulation or by the act. It takes about an hour and a half to fill out the sheet, and then the information given must be wrong, because it almost invariably comes back.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCLUDE CERTAIN CLASSES OF BLIND PERSONS
speechtext: But it does not relate to this act.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCLUDE CERTAIN CLASSES OF BLIND PERSONS
speechtext:
It relates to the carrying
out of the act.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCLUDE CERTAIN CLASSES OF BLIND PERSONS
speechtext: It is not under the act at all.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCLUDE CERTAIN CLASSES OF BLIND PERSONS
speechtext: And as I say, I am not attacking -the minister or-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCLUDE CERTAIN CLASSES OF BLIND PERSONS
speechtext: Or this act.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCLUDE CERTAIN CLASSES OF BLIND PERSONS
speechtext:
I am trying to suggest that the minister should take power to tell the people in British Columbia that if they want to get their money they will have to administer the act according to our act. Is that not a proper idea?
This is some of the information they want: The name of the child; relationship; age; number of dependent children; full address; married, single, widower, or divorced; occupation ; name of employer of each son, daughter or daughter's husband; his employer's address, and his earnings for -the past twelve months. A woman may have a daughter married to a man with six children. They must have information about -his employer, and the employer must put in a return of the employee's wages for the last twelve months, and for the last three months, month by month.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCLUDE CERTAIN CLASSES OF BLIND PERSONS
speechtext: Not under this law, or under the regulations.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCLUDE CERTAIN CLASSES OF BLIND PERSONS
speechtext: That is what I am complaining about. I am glad to hear the minister say it is not under this law.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCLUDE CERTAIN CLASSES OF BLIND PERSONS
speechtext:
I just wish to say that what the hon. member has been saying has not been about the bill now before the house, not with respect to this statute, but with respect to some statute in the province of

Old Age Pensions-Mr. Neill
British Columbia, which, it is true, to a certain extent ties in with the operation of the present old age pension law. That is one of the difficulties which arise where partnership arrangements exist between the dominion and the province. I must say however that it is conveying a false impression, because I think every complaint of the hon. member is with respect to British Columbia administration and British Columbia law, not the law we are discussing to-day.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCLUDE CERTAIN CLASSES OF BLIND PERSONS
speechtext: Then I have totally failed to make my meaning clear. I did mention the British Columbia law, namely the Parents' Maintenance Act, but that was only incidental. Now I am talking, and have been from the start, about the action of the British Columbia board under regulations made by this act.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCLUDE CERTAIN CLASSES OF BLIND PERSONS
speechtext: My hon. friend said it was not under the regulations.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCLUDE CERTAIN CLASSES OF BLIND PERSONS
speechtext: I said it should not be; that is what I meant. Here it is, headed "Old Age Pension Act; application for a pension," and it is done by authority of this act.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCLUDE CERTAIN CLASSES OF BLIND PERSONS
speechtext: No, no.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCLUDE CERTAIN CLASSES OF BLIND PERSONS
speechtext:
And by regulations made
under the act.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCLUDE CERTAIN CLASSES OF BLIND PERSONS
speechtext:
No; the hon. member
forgets there are old age pensions acts in every province, by which each province may authorize its government to enter into an agreement with the government of Canada, under the provisions of the federal act. The province may and often does impose conditions in and for the province which are over and above the conditions imposed by the federal act and the federal agreement.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCLUDE CERTAIN CLASSES OF BLIND PERSONS
speechtext: Again that is not the situation. In the first place, the Old Age Pensions Act provides for agreements to be made between the provinces and the dominion.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCLUDE CERTAIN CLASSES OF BLIND PERSONS
speechtext: Right.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCLUDE CERTAIN CLASSES OF BLIND PERSONS
speechtext: Specifications are made in an agreement which is arrived at, and signed. All a province does is to pass an enabling act, agreeing to the agreement.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCLUDE CERTAIN CLASSES OF BLIND PERSONS
speechtext: No, it is more than that.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCLUDE CERTAIN CLASSES OF BLIND PERSONS
speechtext: It is not permitted under our act to impose any conditions in British Columbia different from those in Alberta. For instance, there could not be a provision for twenty years' residence in Alberta, and ten years' in British Columbia.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCLUDE CERTAIN CLASSES OF BLIND PERSONS
speechtext:
No; with respect to that kind of condition the hon. member is correct.
But my statement is nevertheless correct with respect to conditions other than the one he has mentioned.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCLUDE CERTAIN CLASSES OF BLIND PERSONS
speechtext: The conditions about which I am complaining are not carried out under any British Columbia act. They are carried out under the powers of the federal act. When I say, "Who is administering the Old Age Pensions Act in British Columbia?" I am told it is the board in Vancouver. It is the workmen's compensation board that administers it. They say they are not bound by any law of the province. When they are administering our act they take advantage of the regulations under the act. What I am complaining about is that they go beyond those regulations and1 invent restrictions of their own, which are not under the dominion law or authority at all. That is the point I am trying to make.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCLUDE CERTAIN CLASSES OF BLIND PERSONS
speechtext: But it is not correct.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCLUDE CERTAIN CLASSES OF BLIND PERSONS
speechtext: Our act does not allow them to ask about the earning of a son-in-law; there is no suggestion of that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCLUDE CERTAIN CLASSES OF BLIND PERSONS
speechtext: Would the hon. member permit me to speak?

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCLUDE CERTAIN CLASSES OF BLIND PERSONS
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCLUDE CERTAIN CLASSES OF BLIND PERSONS
speechtext: But the British Columbia Parents' Maintenance Act does allow them. Under the British Columbia law the same board is administering that and other acts for the province.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCLUDE CERTAIN CLASSES OF BLIND PERSONS
speechtext: Yes, but this form I have in my hand is not sent out under the Parents' Maintenance Act.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCLUDE CERTAIN CLASSES OF BLIND PERSONS
speechtext: Oh, well-

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCLUDE CERTAIN CLASSES OF BLIND PERSONS
speechtext: As a matter of fact the Parents' Maintenance Act does not extend to sons-in-law and daughters-in-law. It is the pension board which puts it in, and that is the point of my complaint. I say they are not adhering to the dominion law, they are not adhering to the provincial law; they have a law unto themselves. They are making these fool regulations-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCLUDE CERTAIN CLASSES OF BLIND PERSONS
speechtext: And they are responsible to the government of British Columbia, not to this government.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCLUDE CERTAIN CLASSES OF BLIND PERSONS
speechtext:
When I ask that in British Columbia they say, "Oh, it is under the dominion act; you will have to go to them." I got into trouble with the minister there. He said I had no business going around blaming the province for the way they were carrying out the act, the way the Minister of Finance suggests I should. Then I went over to our Department of Finance and
Old Age Pensions-Mr. Leader

they told me, "We only operate to the extent of seeing that they are making no unjust demands, but we cannot put any pressure upon them to do even what is right." I submitted certain cases to them, and said, "What do you think about these?" They said, "We would pass that in a minute. Why does not British Columbia O.K. it? We would do it." I said, "Can you not make them do it?" and they said, "Our authority goes only to the extent of saying that we will or will not make certain payments. We cannot say that they ought to pay something." I think that is correct-the minister nods his head.
Then I went back to British Columbia, and I was told that that was not so-passing the buck again. They said what their principal object appeared to be, and communicated it in a letter. They boasted that in a number of years past they had never had one case rejected by the dominion authorities, while they could point to other provinces where as many as four hundred had been rejected. The obvious answer was that that was exactly what I was kicking about. Because if a case came within a thousand miles of the limit they would not grant it; that was the trouble, and then they boast that never once were their cases turned down. They are leaning back so far in their fear that the dominion government might possibly refuse a case that they are rejecting cases that the dominion government would be willing to pay. That is one of my complaints.
I have a letter under my hand which I shall not read, but the contents of which I shall state briefly. One of these cases was to be put through, and the board said-not the regulations; not the act-" You must show us what your son-in-law and daughter-in-law earned in the last year, and in the last three months individually." One of the sons was teaching school up in the Peace River district, and it took a lot of time to get word back from him. His school trustee was really in the position of an employer. To shorten the story, may I say that he sent in his income tax return, but the people in Vancouver would not accept it, or the affidavit which came with it. They said they had to have a statement signed by the actual school trustee. By the time that had been accomplished, due to delays in winter service three months had gone by. The board then said, " You sent us in a return for the three individual months of January, February and March, but it is now May; we want another return for February, March and April "-and the whole performance had to be gone through again. Was anybody's interests or property protected by that? No,

it was nothing but red tape from beginning to end.
I wish to bring to the attention of the house something which happened a few years ago under the present leader of the opposition. It will be remembered there was a lot of fuss about soldiers' wives and about red tape causing a great deal of trouble. We asked the right hon. gentleman about it across the floor of the house, and he said he would attend to it. Later in the session he was asked whether he was going to bring in legislation, and he said, "No, I do not think it is necessary; all that is needed is common sense application of the act. I have had a word with the chairman of the board." From that day to this we have had no particular trouble in that connection. It was not the act; it was not the regulation, but it was the foolish way it was carried out by the people concerned. That is the condition in British Columbia. There was an election in British Columbia in 1933 and at that time I told the people that perhaps with a change of government they would get a better deal. There is another election coming on and I am afraid I shall have to tell them the same thing.
I am trying to convey one point to the minister, but I do not appear to have succeeded. I am sorry if I have not succeeded, because I have been desperately in earnest about this matter. I suggest that these people should be told that if they are going to draw funds under this act they must administer the act in a reasonable, decent and common sense way. They must conform with the regulations of the act and not administer it according to their own private opinion. Apparently they have got the tip not to spend more money than they can help, and they are doing that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCLUDE CERTAIN CLASSES OF BLIND PERSONS
speechtext: There was no such tip from here.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCLUDE CERTAIN CLASSES OF BLIND PERSONS
speechtext:
Not from Ottawa, from
Victoria.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCLUDE CERTAIN CLASSES OF BLIND PERSONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if this is the proper time, I should like to make one or two observations. I listened to the remarks of the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill), and if I understood him aright, he is asking that in interpreting the Old Age Pensions Act we should make it easier for the applicants to obtain pensions. I do not see why the authorities should take it for granted that these applicants are committing perjury or stating something which is not in accordance with the truth, especially when the local authorities are there to vouch for the declaration. Instead of making it harder for these people

Old Age Pensions-Mr. Dunning
to get a pension, we should make it a3 easy as possible, provided they are able to fulfil the first requirement of establishing that they are seventy years of age and entitled to a pension.
I understand there is a provision in the Old Age Pensions Act to the effect that an applicant must have lived in the province for five years immediately prior to making his application. There was some reason for that provision when the act was first drafted, because at that time only two or three provinces undertook to work with the dominion. It is quite easy to understand that old people in a province which was not taking advantage of the provisions of the act would drift into one which was. I understand that now all the provinces have come under the provisions of the act. If that is so, I think it should be sufficient when a person proves that he is seventy years of age and has lived in the dominion for twenty years without regard to any particular province. I know of one case where a man eighty years of age who had lived for the last thirty years in Alberta moved into my constituency in order to be near his son. This man is destitute and cannot get a pension because he has not been in Manitoba for five years. Because he preferred to come to Manitoba to be with his son, he cannot get a pension. I do not think that is right.
The other observation I want to make is in connection with the blind. I feel sure the minister will have every sympathy with what I am about (to say. I understand that this bill provides that a blind person applying for pension must have had five years' residence in the province in which application is made. Is that right?
Hon. CHARLES A. DUNNING (Minister of Finance):	Mr. Speaker, I did not expect
that this bill would start a discussion on old age pensions generally. If I had, I would have made a statement in that regard at the outset. I am debarred from speaking now, but I can answer my hon. friend's question very briefly. This bill assumes that a blind person is seventy years of age when he attains the age of forty. That is the sum and substance of it. There are one or two provisions which make it a little more favourable to blind persons than to others, but the main factor is the assumption of the age of seventy when the age of forty is reached. If a discussion is to be permitted on old age pensions generally, I would crave the indulgence of the house to be permitted to make a statement in reply, although I am out of order in so doing.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCLUDE CERTAIN CLASSES OF BLIND PERSONS
speechtext:
I have been requested to
bring this matter before the minister and I am doing it to the best of my ability. I think that anyone labouring under the terrible handicap of blindness should be able to obtain a pension provided he has lived in the dominion, without its being necessary to prove residence of five years in the province immediately prior to his application.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCLUDE CERTAIN CLASSES OF BLIND PERSONS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to make one or two suggestions to the minister and also express one or two thoughts with regard to this bill, which I trust will be helpful to him. I think every hon. member is in favour of the principle of the bill, and I believe it has the support of practically every person in the dominion. The thought in everyone's mind is that it will help a very deserving group of Canadians who are seriously handicapped in their struggle to take a worth while part in the life of the nation. This being the spirit in which the bill is received, I think that now is the time for us to make certain that the administration of the bill and of the Old Age Pensions Act which it amends will not defeat our intentions. We should make sure that the act will be administered in the way in which we intend it to be administered, and in the way in which the people of Canada believe that it will be administered.
This bill provides for pensions for the blind by extending the provisions of the Old Age Pensions Act. When the bill is passed, the Old Age Pensions Act will provide pensions, not only for our elder citizens who have reached the age of seventy years, but also for blind Canadians who have attained the age of forty. Ten years ago when the act was first before the parliament of Canada it received practically unanimous support both from the members of that parliament and from the Canadian people. They had much the same thought in mind as is in our minds to-day, that is, that the legislation would help a deserving group of our people, in that case the needy old who otherwise might be forced to spend their declining years in want and probably in suffering.
My submission is that the old age pension was never intended to be a dole or a form of relief. When the act was passed ten years ago we had no such thing as a dole or no such thing as relief. The old age pension was intended to be a pension payable to a worthy
Old Age Pensions

group of our people. I refer the committee to the terms of section 8 of the Old Age Pensions Act, showing the class of people whom it was expected to help. Under clause (a) a person, in order to get this old age pension, must have been-
... a British subject, or, being a widow, who is not a British subject, was such before her marriage.
Under clause (c), the applicant must have-
. . . resided in Canada for the twenty years immediately preceding the date aforesaid.
And under clause (d) he must have-
. . . resided in the province in which the application for pension is made for the five years immediately preceding the said date.
But by reason of the regulations which were adopted under the Old Age Pensions Act, and the administration of the act and these regulations, the old age pension has come to be considered a form of relief. My suggestion is that that is not good enough, either for British Columbia or for any other province, and I suspect that the conditions are just as bad in the other provinces as they are in British Columbia.

I should like to give the committee a few instances. I must refer of course more particularly to British Columbia. First I would quote regulation 18 (d). That is a regulation passed under the dominion act, not a regulation under an act of a province. It reads as follows:
For the purpose of determining the income of any applicant, the pension authority shall take into account any of the following sources of income:
In British Columbia the pension authority is the board set up by joint action of the provincial and dominion governments.

Salary, wages or other means of livelihood, whether in money or in kind, which the pensioner may reasonably be expected to receive.

Just think what an impossible position it is-that a parent applying for a pension has to go to the son-in-law and ask him for support! Goodness knows how many of his own relations that son-inlaw may be keeping or what his actual financial position may be. The ruling is simply ridiculous. Are the blind people of Canada to be subject to administration of this type? Are they to be subject to similar regulations? If they are, I am afraid they are going to be very much disappointed with this bill.
Then regulation 18 (b) provides that for the purpose of determining the income of any applicant the pension authority shall take into account any of the following sources of income:
(b) Real property at the rate of five per centum of the assessed or market value thereof (whichever be considered the more equitable standard), exclusive of encumbrances.
That, too, is a regulation of the dominion government, passed by the governor in council. I suggest that it is entirely unreasonable. The test should be whether there is any income earned from this property. Why should an old person lose out because he happens to have a vacant lot or a building that he cannot rent? There is no income from either. I suggest that this regulation should be altered. I believe, too, that the applicant for a pension should be allowed to own his or her own home up to a value of, say, $3,500, or, if that is too much, at least to the value of $2,500, and that home should not be taken into consideration in arriving at the amount of the applicant's income.

10.	An applicant may be presumed to have been resident in Canada for the twenty years immediately preceding the date of the proposed commencement of the pension if he-
Then (a) sets out the time he must have lived in Canada:
(b) has not within the said twenty years been absent from Canada for more than 731 consecutive days . . .

If I may be allowed to go on, I wish to speak briefly about the pensions that are payable to people who have been resident in the Yukon. The position with regard to these old Yukoners, old pioneers who went there in 1898, is this. Many of them as they have grown old have broken down and have come out to the cities of Vancouver and Victoria; then after they have been there perhaps six or seven years they reach the age of seventy years and apply for the old age pension, but they are told that though they are seventy and have been in Canada twenty years they can get only $6 or $7, depending on the length of time the applicant has been in British Columbia. The

Old Age Pensions
applicant cannot get anything for the time he has been in the Yukon, because the Old Age Pensions Act does not apply to the Yukon.
I would refer the minister to the report of the Department of Labour for the fiscal year ending March 31, 1935, at page 63:
While legislation was enacted by the Yukon territorial council in 1927, which empowered the gold commissioner of the Yukon territory to enter into an agreement with the governor in council to make the system effective in the territory, the proposed scheme of administration, which must be approved by the governor in council before an agreement can be entered into, has not yet been submitted.
These old Yukoners are being deprived of their full pensions and yet the dominion government would be responsible for seventy-five per cent of the portion of pension which they cannot draw. Furthermore, I believe that the dominion government would be required to pay the whole thing because they finance relief in the Yukon. I put a question to the Minister of Mines and Resources (Mr. Crerar) last year and I would refer the committee to page 2782 of Hansard:
Mr. Green:	If the old age pension scheme
were made effective in the Yukon territory, where would the money come from? Would that money be raised by the Yukon territorial council or would it come from the dominion government? As the minister knows, the provinces pay one-quarter of the old age pension. If the scheme were made effective in the Yukon, where would that one-quarter come from?
Mr. Crerar: It would come from the territorial government, and I assume in the last analysis it might really be provided for by the federal government.
Mr. Green:	The federal government would
really have to pay the whole shot.
Mr. Crerar:	It is federal government territory.
Mr. Green:	That would not come out of
local taxes raised by the Yukon council.
Mr. Crerar:	I could not say, speaking
offhand.
I suggest that these Yukoners are being deprived by the national government of the pittance which the people of Canada expected would be paid to them and which they believe is being paid. In my opinion the Old Age Pension Act should be made applicable in the Yukon from now on and provision should be made for paying the full pension to those whose applications have already been dealt with.
When the Old Age Pensions Act was passed it provided that the dominion should pay half the cost of pensions and the provinces half. In 1931 the late government increased the contribution of the dominion to three-fourths and provided for the examination and audit of all expenditures by the provinces and 31111-1151
of the accounts of the provinces. This means that this national parliament is the body most directly concerned in the administration of the old Age Pensions Act and further that this parliament must assume the bulk of the responsibility for the administration of the act. Certainly we are going to take the whole of the blame if the act is not properly administered.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCLUDE CERTAIN CLASSES OF BLIND PERSONS
speechtext: That is very evident.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCLUDE CERTAIN CLASSES OF BLIND PERSONS
speechtext: My suggestion to the minister is this-and I believe it is a constructive suggestion-that he should have a thorough investigation made at once into the administration of the Old Age Pensions Act in the different provinces, and that he then make any necessary changes in the regulations and in the administration. I would suggest further that that investigation be not made by a commission-we have had enough commissions, for a time at least. I suggest that it be made by an official of the department. I have far more confidence in the department-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCLUDE CERTAIN CLASSES OF BLIND PERSONS

This government should spare no effort to make sure that the intention of parliament and of the Canadian people is carried out in the administration of the Old Age Pensions Act, namely, not that the act should be used to provide relief or a dole, but that it should help to make the lives of our blind people and the last years of our own old people happier than they have been.

However, it is well to bear in mind that this act came into operation not quite ten years ago. It was in a way new legislation-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCLUDE CERTAIN CLASSES OF BLIND PERSONS

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCLUDE CERTAIN CLASSES OF BLIND PERSONS
speechtext: When the Old Age Pensions Act was framed it was something new as far as Canada was concerned. Something had to be done to overcome the difficulties inherent in our constitution. I have no doubt that many of the regulations which have proven so irksome to some are the result of constitutional difficulties. The five year residence clause was one of the problems which provoked a good deal of thought and discussion at the time. But in view of the fact that all the provinces, with the possible exception of one, have adopted the principle of old age pension legislation and have come under the act, I feel that now is the time for the government to see whether changes could not be made in the regulations, as suggested by the hon. member for Vancouver South.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCLUDE CERTAIN CLASSES OF BLIND PERSONS
speechtext: The agreement is for ten years.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCLUDE CERTAIN CLASSES OF BLIND PERSONS

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCLUDE CERTAIN CLASSES OF BLIND PERSONS
speechtext:
I know four of them

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCLUDE CERTAIN CLASSES OF BLIND PERSONS
speechtext: The five year clause?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCLUDE CERTAIN CLASSES OF BLIND PERSONS
speechtext: Yes, for obvious reasons. I know British Columbia would object because it would tend to increase the load on that province, which is a more desirable place for old people to live than some other parts of Canada. That is the whole story. The provinces consider these matters in relation to their own peculiar interests. I know, because I have discussed it with them.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCLUDE CERTAIN CLASSES OF BLIND PERSONS
speechtext: I remember some arguments being used in this chamber about ten years ago-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCLUDE CERTAIN CLASSES OF BLIND PERSONS
speechtext:
It is not argument. I
have discussed that possibility with the provinces.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCLUDE CERTAIN CLASSES OF BLIND PERSONS
speechtext:
Well, it is an argument controverted by the facts, because the percentage of old age pensioners in British Columbia is no greater than it is in other provinces. If the five year residence clause were abolished I doubt whether many old people would care to leave the old homesteads and familiar surroundings for the purpose of living in British Columbia. The number of pensioners in British Columbia at the present time is no greater proportionately than in Manitoba; in fact the most recent figures I could get showed that the number was somewhat less in British Columbia. If the minister through his department would confer with the provinces and see whether something could be done along that line, I would be content to abide by the decision so arrived at, and if the provinces objected to the deletion of the five year residence clause we in this chamber would have nothing further to say.
Another matter which the minister might take into consideration, and one that creates a good deal of feeling amongst prospective or actual recipients of old age pensions, is the right of provincial authorities to put a lien on property in the possession of pensioners. I do not know whether this would apply to the blind; if not, I need not refer to it, but if it does, the argument applies. Suppose an old person is in possession of property worth $2,000 or $3,000-I have known of many such instances. He may have a small home which he has owned for twenty or thirty or forty years, but before he is entitled to receive the benefit of the Old Age Pensions Act he is compelled to assign that property over to the provincial authorities. I do not think this parliament desires to be so harsh with old people as to compel them to give up such small properties. Many old people, being loath to part with their little possessions, resort to subterfuge in order to evade

Old Age Pensions
that provision. I am wondering whether we could not be a little more generous now than we were in 1926 or 1927, and abolish that regulation.
Another point which I think also comes under the present bill relates to the question of earnings. Under the existing legislation a recipient of old age pension is allowed an income of $125 a year over and above his pension. He is entitled to have a total income of $365 a year, including $240 pension. If the pensioner has an income of $200 a year over and above his pension, the amount of pension is reduced. I think that restriction on the earnings of pensioners should be done away with. They should be entitled to a larger income under the act, and the same should apply in respect of the blind people who may come under the present proposals. I draw this to the attention of the minister and the government. I know they are sympathetic and I appreciate the bringing in of this legislation. It is one of the best things they have done since they came into office; for although the number of pensioners may not be great, it is because of the principle embodied, and the satisfaction it will give to so many people, that the bill has been received with interest and approval throughout the length and breadth of Canada.
May I say one further word. As I pointed out a moment ago, this bill is something new so far as this country is concerned, just as the old age pension legislation was something new when it was brought in. At that time the government had to find ways and means of overcoming the difficulties presented by the British North America Act, so they took the course of making an agreement under which the provinces could come under the provisions of the bill. Where there was a will there was a way, and I am pointing this out to the house and to the government for the simple reason that if there is the will to overcome the difficulties inherent under our constitution, ways and means can be found just as a way was found to bring in old age pension legislation. If our government really desired to bring in other social legislation, which is long overdue in this country-such as unemployment insurance, minimum wages and maximum hours of labour-they could find ways of overcoming the difficulties in that connection also.
Hon. CHARLES A. DUNNING (Minister of Finance): I wonder if I might be permitted now to say a few of the things I might have said on the second reading of the bill, and possibly thereby shortened the
discussion. What has been said causes me to preface my remarks by saying that more than 150,000 people in Canada are now receiving old age pensions.

speechtext: Has the minister the exact number?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCLUDE CERTAIN CLASSES OF BLIND PERSONS
speechtext:
I have not the exact number, because Quebec just came in a few months ago, and is adding to the number very rapidly month by month. We are anticipating some thirty thousand from that province by the end of April, which would bring the total closer to 160,000 people who are in receipt of old age pensions.
I think it is proper for the minister whose unpleasant duty it is to try to guard the treasury to point to that fact in view of the discussion which has taken place to-day, which to a casual listener would indicate that the Dominion of Canada has not been carrying out properly or generously the provisions of the law. The amount which will be required from the federal treasury commencing on the first of next month in order to pay old age pensions during that year will be $27,500,000. With these figures before it, Mr. Chairman, I think the committee will at least reach the conclusion that the cases which have been cited this afternoon by practically every previous speaker must be the exception rather than the rule, and that there is a much more humanitarian administration of old age pensions generally across Canada than the discussion in this house this afternoon would lead one to believe. The fact that we have so many people getting old age pensions is to my mind an evidence of the absolute lack of recognition of moral obligation by the children of those who are receiving the pension. They lose entirely that sense of obligation to their fathers and mothers that was possessed by the children of two or three generations ago. To my mind, the reason for that is that perhaps we are indulging in too much paternalism in this country. There is no sense of obligation on the part of sons and daughters to-day, at any rate in a great number of instances,
Old Age Pensions

and the sooner a sense of responsibility is brought home to them the better it will be for themselves, for their parents, and for the morale of the people in general.
The Minister of Finance has told us that as the years pass we are going to have an increased burden in connection with the pas'-ment of pensions. It seems to me that we tackle the thing at the wrong end. Why are so many people blind? In the. schools for the blind in London, England, fifty per cent of those who are there are there because of venereal disease. What is this country doing, either through the Department of National Health or through the provincial departments of health, to educate the people so that they may ward off these diseases? We discuss the little tutti-frutti grants from the federal government to the national institute for the blind, and give only S13.000 for maternal and child welfare and to carry on education at a time when it is needed and when it might prevent that blindness. In that regard I think we should be much more careful than we are in the medical examination of prospective immigrants to Canada. If we are to cut down the ever increasing sum which it will take to pay pensions to the blind we must start a good deal further back and do something towards the prevention of those diseases that contribute so largely to blindness.
I am not in favour of the policy of this or any other government paying seventy-five per cent of the total expenditures and not having under its jurisdiction complete control of the expenditure of that money. It makes no difference whether you hand it over to a Liberal administration in Ontario or Quebec or to any other type of administration of whatever political colour. When you are paying 75 per cent of the money you should have complete and absolute control of how it is to be spent. If politics are entering into the administration, it is because provincial governments say:	The
dominion is paying 75 per cent; we are paying only 25 per cent, and heretofore we have passed on part of that to the municipalities; we can use it as a political lever. The whole system needs revamping, and anything we can do to prevent the diseases which cause blindness and to control the expenditure of the moneys which we collect from the people in taxes will be a step in the right direction.

In fact, it has made it impossible for people to provide for themselves in their youth and manhood; so how can they provide for old age? Not very long ago people working on a farm were able to do a little useful work until they died, but such is not the case to-day. If you read any of the reports of industrial institutions you will find that to-day people are put out of industrial employment, not at the age of sixty-five or seventy, but at the age of forty-five, and their chances of getting into employment again if they lose their jobs at that age are very slight. There are three points to which I wish to direct attention. The first is, can anything be done to provide for reciprocal benefits with respect to old age pensions? That is, to provide for our citizens continuing to receive old age pension if they go to England, and for New Zealanders, say, coming here still to receive the old age pension on the same conditions as would be granted to a Canadian who might go to New Zealand. I found that question engaging the attention of our friends in the Antipodes, and it has frequently been brought to my attention in connection with aged men and women who would like to go back to the homeland and die beside the old home. They cannot now carry with them their pension, but reciprocal arrangements might be provided. The matter has been considered, and I think there must be a considerable volume of correspondence in respect to it. I was going to ask whether it has been advanced any further than when I last knew of it.
The second point relates to the Yukon, to which reference has already been made. In the Northwest Territories seven pensions are being paid, and seven only. The Minister of Labour of that day, Mr. Heenan, thought he had accomplished a great deal when he negotiated an agreement with the government of the Northwest Territories, and it was spoken of in terms quite complimentary to the minister. Might I suggest that the position of the Yukon is somewhat stronger than that of the Northwest Territories. I think no one knows that better than the minister, because I gathered from something he said the other day that he had been giving attention to it personally and knew something of the number of people who would be affected.
The third point has to do with the administration of the act. No one who has been in the Finance department, as I was until 1932, would deny that the act has been badly administered. I wholly agree with what the minister said, and when I took steps to have the administration placed under the Minister of Finance-I had forgotten for the moment

little. But, Mr. Chairman, there was still much to do when I last dealt with the matter, and the minister says there is still much to do. The reason is that we have not sufficient control. We can say this is a fraud or that is a fraud, but when you send men to remote sections of this country to check up these things, just watch the difficulties they encounter. When I saw the reports that came back from some of the men we sent out I began to realize for the first time the magnitude of the difficulties that confronted them in endeavouring to check these reports.
I recall very vividly the discussion in this house when this statute was passed providing for an agreement for ten years, not longer. It was to be experimental, and we were to pay fifty per cent of the cost. Subsequently we increased our contribution to seventy-five per cent, because the provinces were clamouring for more revenue and larger payments. The matter got into the realm of politics, just as it did in Australia and in Germany. The first old age pension act of Bismarck became a matter of political discussion very soon after it was introduced. The questions raised were two. They were the subject of agitation in Australia, and they are beginning to be the subject of discussion here. They are, first, the reduction of the age when pension will be paid to sixty-five or sixty; and, secondly, the increase of the benefits beyond $20 per month. Those are the same problems wrestled' with in Germany, and later in Australia. As a matter of fact in Australia one government was defeated practically on that issue, though not wholly.
What did1 we do? We passed a statute that provided definitely that if one had attained a certain age, under certain other conditions which I need not take time to repeat, he or she was entitled to benefits; and unless there was compliance with those conditions, benefits were not payable. My colleague from Leeds made that abundantly clear. But human nature is human nature, and at the very beginning people began to say, Well, they are inquiring about my age, but my age is all right, and I have been quite a number of years in this country now. My hon. friend from Rosthern (Mr. Tucker) referred to a case, and I know of one somewhat similar. This man left the country and went to California, with no intention of ever returning. But the depression came along and he was practically driven out of California, so he came back and said: Oh, that was only a temporary absence and it should not count. There are many cases of that kind; I fancy there is not a member of this committee who does not know of them.

Then there is the other question, of age. It is said that the provinces are very stiff in requiring evidence of age. Well, those who have had to do with life insurance companies, and who know anything of the claims that are made on the basis of the establishment of age, will realize the ease with which people will stretch their imagination and advance or lessen their age as may be desirable. Those are facts; we have evidence of them right here in this house.
I think this committee should give the minister every possible support in the discharge of a most difficult task. If I say I know what that task is, I am but repeating what the minister himself has said. Perhaps I would not have referred to it if he had not done so, but I think we can purge these lists of a very substantial number of names. I regret to say that, but I think I know what I am speaking of when I say that the lists in some of the provinces could be reduced quite substantially. The other question, having to do with the means test, is of course one about which there may be differences of opinion.

Mr. Chairman, may I say at the outset without hesitation that I believe the Old Age Pensions Act has been administered without the slightest political tendency. I believe the head of our board, Mr. Blois, who was formerly a judge of the juvenile court, is absolutely impartial and absolutely fair in the administration of the funds which come under his control.
I have an idea that the Old Age Pensions Act should be administered and supported entirely by the dominion government, and I took that position before the original bill was introduced. At that time I was provincial secretary of Nova Scotia, and when consulted by the then Minister of Labour I said on behalf of the government of Nova Scotia that we did not propose to enter into any contributory scheme on a fifty-fifty basis, because the government of that province could not afford to make the contribution. Hon. members will recall that Nova Scotia did not enter into any agreement with the dominion until 1933.
I am amused at the turn which matters sometimes take in a discussion of this kind. I have had experiences somewhat like those of

the hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Stewart). People have come to me and asked me to fill out applications. I have been told: My neighbour was a good Conservative and was getting an old age pension; why cannot I get one? I have been told plainly that I did not stand in well with the government, or otherwise the pension would go through. I had to tell this man that I did not know how the other man had secured his pension, but the probabilities were that he had not made a proper return. I told him I could not advise him to make an incorrect return, as that would not be worth doing. I said that if on a correct return he was entitled to a pension, I was quite sure the board would see that he got whatever he was entitled to under the regulations.
Something has been said about pensions being paid to the inmates of poorhouses. These pensions are of no benefit to the provincial government of Nova Scotia, as these institutions are supported by the municipalities. I had an experience with an inmate of one of these institutions. I told him I was surprised that he was looking for an old age pension, as I knew what he had received for a farm he had sold not more than a year before. He has not put in his application yet, but he is all ready to do so.
I believe the act is administered with reasonable honesty in Nova Scotia. The gentleman at the head of the department is conscientious and very capable. However, I am afraid that some of the inspectors who take applications throughout the province are not as careful in collecting data as they might be. I believe pensions are being paid in the province which should not be paid, but I suppose this is true of all provinces.

As the hon. member for Grey-Bruce (Miss Macphail) has said, I do not know how we could have got through the years of depression without this act being in force.

sometimes in order that pensions may be obtained by certain people. I know that in my own province many farmers and others signed over their property to their children just before the Old Age Pensions Act came into force in order to become eligible for a pension. I give a great deal of credit to the Hon. George S. Henry, former Premier of Ontario and Minister of Highways, for rechecking the pension lists. Many names were struck off, as it was found that many people who had lots of money to live on had been trying to impose on the public.
I do not agree entirely with the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill) as to red tape in granting pensions. I think what is needed is a wider interpretation of the act. The boards should cut out a lot of red tape and administer the act in a businesslike manner. They should not try to inconvenience or humiliate an applicant for a pension, but at the same time the treasury of this country should be protected to see that it is not drained dry. It seems to me that everyone is after the Minister of Finance for something.
I do not agree with the provision in the act that a man receiving a pension of $20 a month cannot earn over $100 a year. That provision should be changed. A man of seventy or seventy-five years of age should be entitled to make a few dollars to buy himself some little luxuries. I think such a man should be allowed to earn more than $100 per year before his pension is reduced.

May I follow the example of others in offering a suggestion for discussion at the coming conference with the provinces concerning , old age pensions. I have in mind two cases which I think are of sufficient importance to establish principles as others may be similarly circumstanced. They have to do with the matter of desertion. In, one case, a lady, a pioneer in this country, went out to western Canada when she was very young, and got married in her later years. After she had become quite elderly her husband* left her and returned to France. 3he had no word from him for, I believe, six years. She then became destitute and tried to secure the old age pension. The department required assurance that the husband was either dead or presumed to be dead. An investigation was made and, unfortunately, the husband was discovered to be living in France, with the result that his wife is debarred from securing the old age pension in this country. If he had not been found, or could have been presumed to be dead, or had been dead, the lady would have been entitled to an old* age pension.
The other case is of a similar kind. A French Canadian woman moved out to western Canada in her early years and there

married a Swedish citizen. Before he was married he acquired Canadian citizenship, in fact, he took out a homestead in this country and farmed it for a number of years. Then, because of family quarrels or perhaps for other reasons, he left this country and returned to Sweden. It is now two and a half years since the case was brought to my attention, and we have been trying to find out the circumstances of the husband. I am told that if he has again applied for Swedish nationality his wife can revert to her Canadian status and become eligible for an old age pension; but if he has not done so, although he may remain in Sweden, she cannot qualify for a pension. Perhaps the principles which are involved in these cases could be dealt with when the minister meets with the provincial representatives to reconsider this legislation.

Central Finance Corporation
I have no interest financial or otherwise in this corporation except in so far as it benefits the borrowers of money on the plan set out. There is a large body of people whose borrowings are not attractive to our banking institutions. The bill admirably provides for exactly that type of borrower.
I am not asking that the house pass the bill. I am simply requesting that it be referred to the standing committee on banking and commerce where it may be thoroughly discussed.
The Central Finance Corporation was the first loan organization to ask for and secure government supervision, control and regulation of its business. Ft has by far the largest investment, and the most complete statistics in regard to this kind of business in the dominion. It was incorporated in 1928 by a special act of the Canadian parliament, which defines and limits its powers. I might give a typical example to show how some of our bootlegging finance corporations have been carrying on business in Canada.
I have here information with regard to one company making loans, including the sum of $200. The borrower receives $209 in cash, for which he pays $135 in charges, repayable in equal monthly payments over a period of one year. The rate charged by the lender was 124-4 per cent per annum or $10.38 a month. This is the very condition which this legislation is designed to end. Under the terms of Bill C the legal charges permitted on such a loan would have been $29.28 instead of $135. The charges indicated are not uncommon among unregulated lenders in all parts of the country, and unless this legislation is passed, permitting a rate sufficient to compensate for the expense in making these small loans, but preventing exorbitant rates of profits, the needy borrower who cannot qualify for a bank loan will have no alternative but to patronize these so-called bootlegger organizations and pay bootleg prices.
I have here a copy of the Toronto Star under date March 15, 1937, and there are twelve of these companies advertising small loans. There are only two of them under government regulation and control. I have another paper which is well known to some members of the house, the Toronto Telegram, and it carries advertisements from thirteen of these firms, only two of them being under government control.
My suggestion is that this bill be treated the same as the bill that was presented to the house last Friday evening; that is to say, that it be sent to the standing committee on banking and commerce, where it may be thoroughly discussed. To my mind the question is not whether this bill is right or wrong.
31111-110J
The point is, does the house desire to have the bill considered in committee where it may be thoroughly discussed? I for one am eager to eliminate loan companies operating without jurisdiction and imposing any excessive burden of interest. I am satisfied that this bill is at least a step in the right direction, and hence my reason for requesting that it be referred to the standing committee on banking and commerce.
Contrary to the general opinion, all members of the house have the privilege of attending the committee and participating in its discussions, and also the right to ask questions. In other words, they have the same privileges as the members of the committee, except that they have no vote. Furthermore, Mr. Finlayson, an official of the finance department, whose duty it is to protect the general public in matters of finance and interest, is also in attendance at the committee. I therefore move that this bill be referred to the standing committee on .banking and commerce where it may receive attention without delay.

speechtext:
I sincerely hope that this bill will not be dealt with in exactly the same manner as the bill which was discussed on Friday night. This bill embodies certain decidedly objectionable features, and it seems to me regrettable that the stamp of the house should be placed upon it by giving it second reading and so perpetuating what may be termed shady business practices through various obnoxious features incorporated in the bill.
I would remind the house that this problem has faced hon. members for a number of years, and it has been generally agreed that the situation reveals that the people who must apply for loans to companies of this character are those who cannot obtain credit from chartered banks. They usually obtain these small loans when facing emergent circumstances such as death or sickness, when they cannot lodge any effective protest against the extortionate terms demanded by companies of this sort. I consider it highly significant that the amending bill is now brought before parliament because of certain objections lodged by the superintendent of insurance. I gather from evidence given before committees of parliament that the superintendent objected to the procedure followed .by the company in demanding a fee of ten dollars in respect of all chattel mortgages. This particular company, I understand, specializes in a loan business in connection with which security is required under chattel mortgage.

Central Finance Corporation
Some irregularity was alleged concerning the fees they were charging, there being a maximum fee of $10 whether or not any actual disbursement had been made. I understand there is some doubt whether the annual licence may be renewed because of this alleged irregularity.
Furthermore, the explanatory notes attached to the bill are grossly misleading. They would lead one to believe that the company is voluntarily reducing the rates of interest. Opposite page 3 the note reads in part:
The maximum rate of charge provided in the bill is lower than the present maximum and constitutes a reduction in rate on the majority of loans made.
Lower down it states:
Two rates are suggested because the ordinary endorsed loan business costs less to operate than a chattel loan business.
It goes on to say:
The personal loan department of the Canadian Bank of Commerce is at present doing an endorsed loan business at an effective rate of slightly over 1 per centum per month.
We find upon examination of section 5 as it at present stands, that under its present charter, the company may charge a discount of 7 per cent. Referring to section 5 (i), the company may:
(i) lend money secured by assignment of choses-in-action, chattel mortgages or such other evidence of indebtedness as the company may require, and may charge interest thereon at the rate of not more than seven per centum per annum and may deduct such interest in advance and provide for repayment in weekly, monthly or other uniform repayments;
In addition, under subsection (ii) the company is empowered to charge:
-in addition to interest as aforesaid, for all expenses which have been necessarily and in good faith incurred by the company in making a loan authorized by the next preceding subparagraph (i), including all expenses for inquiry and investigation into character and circumstances of the borrower, his co-maker or surety, for taxes, correspondence and professional advice and for all necessary documents and papers, two per centum upon the principal sum loaned;
That means a total discount of 9 per cent, or an effective interest rate of 18 per cent per annum, or 1^ per cent per month. That, of course, is exclusive of the charge made for the chattel mortgage fee.
Under existing legislation no company is now permitted to charge more than 1^ per cent per month on the unpaid balance of loans of $500 or less. I am referring to the Loan Companies Act. The amending section provides a fixed rate of 1^ per cent:
(a) on loans made in whole or in part upon the security of co-makers, endorsers, sureties or guarantors other than one only of the follow-
(Mr. MacNeil.l
ing, the wife, husband, brother, sister or child of the borrower, at a rate not exceeding one and one-half per centum per month on the unpaid principal balance owing by the borrower.
And subsection Ob):
On loans made without security or secured in any manner permitted by this act other than the manner described in the next preceding subparagraph (a) of this section, at a rate not exceeding two and one-quarter per centum per month on the unpaid principal balances owing by the borrower.
The proposed change, instead of lowering the interest rate, will increase the charges by 50 per cent from 18 per cent to a rate of approximately 27 per cent per annum. That is, the rate will be increased by | of 1 per cent per month. Therefore I submit that the explanatory notes attached to this bill are grossly misleading, and this house should not countenance any such misrepresentation of the facts.
For many reasons this bill does not stand in the relationship of a private bill because of the discussion that has taken place during the years, and the likelihood that endorsement by second reading will be regarded as establishing vested privileges for companies of this character. I submit that such legislation should not be approved until a thorough investigation has been made of the whole problem. I suggest that such investigation might properly be conducted by a royal commission. The only evidence yet heard on this subject has been the evidence secured from the loan companies; no evidence has yet been heard from the borrowers before committee of this house. I find that assurances have been given in the past on this score. At page 3550 of Hansard of 1936 the present Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning), discussing a similar bill, said:
It is evident, Mr. Speaker, that this matter of interest rates and the conditions applying to small loans must again engage the attention of parliament. It is the intention of the government to initiate, between now and the next session of parliament, a further examination of the matter with a view to amending the existing general legislation. In the meantime I must oppose the second reading of the bill now before the house which, to summarize, provides for effective annual rates of interest ranging from 24i per cent up to 94 per cent. I am sure that the bouse will regard such rates as excessive. It is true that in the general legislation now governing the matter the rates are expressed in terms of monthly rates, but there are various other charges, such as chattel mortgages and so forth, which operate to add to the annual interest charge or the monthly interest charge which the borrower has to pay. In connection with this bill and the one that follows, the government suggests that the house should reject them at this

Central Finance Corporation
session on the principle that we should not incorporate any more companies of this kind until the general legislation can be brought more into harmony with present day conditions, so far as the cost of money is concerned.
I submit that although this company is already incorporated and operating in the dominion, the same argument applies, particularly in view of the objections which have been raised by the superintendent of insurance regarding its operations.
The matter was thoroughly discussed in the session of 1934. I find that on that occasion the then Prime Minister, the present leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) said in part, referring to the practice in other countries:
As they are the subject matter of much legislation in various countries my own view is that the enactment of this amendment will protect the public in the meantime, and that we could pass at next session of parliament a money lenders' act modelled along the general principle of the British legislation.
Further he says:
Under the circumstances I desire to assure the hon. member for Macleod that it is my intention to proceed with this bill immediately the opportunity offers, and to make all companies, which heretofore have been, are being or may hereafter be incorporated, subject to it. The limitation mentioned in the bill is 2 per cent, but after reading the British Money Lenders Act, and other legislation, I may say that when the time comes we may adopt a rate of 2J per cent instead of 2 per cent.
But the assurance was given then, and subsequently, that the whole problem would be reviewed and legislation would be introduced governing the general practice. I think it was the intention of those who spoke on that occasion that such general legislation would to some extent govern companies obtaining charters under provincial legislation, such companies, it was alleged, being guilty of more serious sharp practice than has been attributed to companies such as the one now under discussion. It is interesting to note, during the discussion which took place in the session of 1934, as reported at page 4479 of Hansard, the advertising conducted on behalf of some of these companies. The then member for Macleod spoke of circular letters received headed, "Keep on the sunny side," with the text reading as follows:
Harassed by petty debts?
Are they impairing your ability to work? Clear them all this simple way.
Figure up how much you owe-then come to the Industrial Loan. We will advance you sufficient to pay them all at once. Take a year to repay us in small monthly instalments.
Do it now! Free your mind of worries and get out of debt on the convenient thrift plan. You will be surprised how easy and simple it is for any salaried man or woman to obtain a loan from $50 to $500 or more.
If you are keeping house and are able to make regular monthly repayments, you have all the security necessary for a loan. No negotiable collateral or real estate are required, the only signatures necessary are those of husband and wife.
Simplicity is the keynote of the thrift plan.
And the hon. member went on to say:
ic Then at the bottom appear the words, "Industrial Loan and Finance Corporation," and in brackets the words "under dominion government supervision." Then the circular goes on to give the name of the manager and the address of the Ottawa office. Then, in the corner, under the very pretty title of "Keep on the sunny side," I find the following:
Personal loans from $50 to $500.
1.	The only investigations made are the questions asked of you.
2.	The only signatures needed are those of husband and wife.
3.	Lowest charge in Canada on loans of this type-our rate authorized by a special act of the dominion parliament incorporating the company.
He added:
My reason for bringing this circular to the attention of the Prime Minister and the government is to suggest that in some section of the bill we should incorporate a paragraph which would limit the type of advertising these companies may carry on.
Then he says:
I certainly think some of this advertising is misleading.
I submit that a bill of this kind tends to nullify existing legislation. I refer to the Money-Lenders Aot, which forbids a rate of interest in excess of 12 per cent per annum in respect of loans of less than $500. This act has been honoured more in the breach than in the observance. As far as I can ascertain no definite attempt has been made to enforce this provision in connection with loan companies, all of which goes to show the need for a thorough investigation of the whole problem at this time.
As I have already said, the bill now before us distinguishes between two classes of loans, those secured by endorsement, and those secured by chattel mortgage. I understand that this company specializes in loans on chattel mortgages, and does very little business on loans secured by endorsements. By the explanatory note they would have us believe that the reduction to one and a half per cent in one instance, and two and a quarter per cent in the other, represents a general reduction in the gross revenue from loans, but this is of little significance when you consider that practically no business is done by this company on the basis of personal endorsements.

Central Finance Corporation
Furthermore, Mr. Speaker, the provisions of this bill make it liable .to grave abuses. The parent company, to which the sponsor of the bill has referred, has stated very definitely on more than one occasion in the United States that it cannot profitably make loans of less than 8200 at a lower rate than 2| per cent per month. If the fixed rate suggested in this bill is secured, no doubt the Canadian company will follow the practice that has been adopted in the United States and refuse to make loans for sums of less than $200, confining .their operations to the more profitable field of loans between $300 and $500.
Furthermore, I am reliably informed that when an applicant goes to an office of this company, having been attracted by the advertisement stating that loans may be secured ait the exceptionally low rate of per cent per month, he is persuaded by various means to take a loan on the security of a chattel mortgage rather than on a personal endorsement. In discussing matters with the applicant the official usually informs him that of course they will make the loan at li .per cent if he secures more than one endorser, say his brother and another individual, but he cannot get the advantage of that low rate without the second endorsement. Then it is explained to the applicant that under the circumstances he can obtain a loan of, say $500 if he gives a chattel mortgage, and human nature being what it is, the applicant usually accepts the loan at an interest rate of or 21 per cent. I am informed also that the chattel mortgage given as security is usually for an amount far in excess of the total loan, so if through some further mischance foreclosure should be executed, the borrower is practically ruined.
I suggest that this paves the way to grave abuses. I believe public opinion demands an investigation such as I have urged, and I understand that on more than one occasion the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) has received petitions from representative groups of people urging that a royal commission be appointed to investigate the whole question.
