The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) made what I thought was a very sensible suggestion when he pointed out the futility, until this bill reached the committee of discussing the bill which is now before the committee, and which, while not in all respects the same, nevertheless involves the principle with which this bill deals. I concurred with the hon. gentleman in that view, and the discussion was more or less suspended.
I had another reason for taking that position. Since the previous discussion in this house I have received a communication from the credit unions in the maritime provinces asking for an opportunity to present their point of view to the committee with respect to this whole matter. As I indicated last week, my interest in this question arises largely because of my belief in the real merit of the credit unions themselves. While I realize that the sphere of the credit unions is not altogether the same as that of these companies, I think the time involved considering this whole matter might .be spent wisely and with great advantage.
There is a further reason. It strikes me that a parliament such as this would be eminently unfair if it gave one bill the privilege of full consideration by a committee while denying that privilege to another similar bill. While these bills may differ in some of their details the same principle is involved, and I do not think it would be fair to discuss one bill without at the same time discussing the other. On that ground alone, Mr. Speaker, I believe this bill should be referred to the committee.
There is also a further reason. The hon. gentleman who has just spoken (Mr. MacNeil) quite properly pointed to the need of an investigation into this whole question. The other night the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) gave reasons which, with his knowledge of the situation, he considered good

Central Finance Corporation
reasons for not holding that general investigation at the present time. Personally I should like to see such an inquiry held, but I must take the minister's view that this is not the time for it. Failing that, is there not more to be gained by considering this matter in committee than by merely taking the attitude that it should not be discussed at all? Giving the bill second reading does not mean that the bill is adopted. I do not know whether or not I am in favour of the bill. I see some merits in it and a good many objectionable features, but all those can be brought out in committee.
This morning the superintendent of insurance appeared before the committee and discussed the general problem of borrowing, having in mind these two bills. There is no opportunity in this house of examining the superintendent of insurance; there is no opportunity of finding out what he thinks of credit unions; there is no opportunity of finding out what he thinks would be a proper relationship between credit unions as existing in the maritime provinces and the caisse populaire in Quebec. Failing a royal commission, the very examination which the hon. member is urging should be pursued in the banking and commerce committee. If this is not done, I want to point out to the hon. member what he is doing. The situation in respect to borrowing and lending is this: Human nature being what it is, the need for credit seems necessarily always to pursue individuals.
I agree with the remarks of the hon. member for Kootenay East (Mr. Stevens) when the other evening he took the view, having in mind this constant demand for credit and the classes of people who must look for credit, that possibly the time had come when the state should set up organizations to extend credit to people with low incomes. I agree with that suggestion, but I do not think that to-day it is possible to attain it. I do not want to criticize the government of the day. While I cannot speak for it, I do not suppose it would :be prepared to accept the suggestion. Failing that, to dismiss this bill in the summary fashion in which the hon. member would have it dismissed would be to place the whole question of borrowing and lending in the hands of people who now escape supervision and regulation.
The sponsor of the bill pointed out that in current numbers of two of the Toronto papers several companies engaged in the business of lending sums from $500 down did so in every instance but one without being subject to any
kind of regulation. Why? Because they operate in two ways, either under provincial charters, where there are no regulations, or without charters at all.

companies increased so much that in the state of Maryland, and I believe also in the state of New York, the legislatures increased the rates, and the actual result was a decrease in the number of illegitimate companies operating. If the ordinary man with a small income can get money from companies such as those dealt with in these bills at a rate of interest lower than he can from the scabs or sharks, that is where he is going to go.
Speaking on this question the other night the right hon. leader of the opposition said his researches into the work of the Sage foundation-and I wish to be quite fair in quoting him-resulted in showing abuses of the very kind then under discussion in the house. It is not a question of our approving the present situation or saying that it is the best. People will continue to borrow. They have always borrowed, and while it may be desirable to set up an agency where they can borrow at the lowest possible rate of interest, one has to recognize not so much what is desirable but what is immediately possible. If this measure were killed a difficult situation would arise. I made the statement the other night, on the basis of information I received from the superintendent of insurance, that some 30,000 outstanding loans not now paid by borrowers would thereby be affected. I have since learned from the superintendent of insurance that during the past four years some $15,000,000 have been loaned by this particular company. Just think what that means. If we dropped this measure suddenly we would only be placing a great burden on this company, and more particularly upon the borrowers.
The real issue in my opinion is this: A bill involving in substance this same principle has been referred to a committee. I supported the suggestion of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) to the effect that our committee discussion might better take place on both bills together. With him, I should like to see this bill referred to the committee, in order that the borrowers might be given the opportunity to present their point of view. I would suggest that we bring representatives here of the Russell Sage foundation, also the superintendent of insurance, and I personally would like to bring two individuals from my own constituency who have suffered from the operations of this

very kind of a company which will be protected unless we exercise some measure of regulation.
While I do not think this is a full and proper way of regulating, yet under the circumstances and having in mind the observations of the Minister of Finance I would say it is the only way left open. I ask the hon. member who has just spoken to consider seriously what the results of his suggestion if adopted would be. In any event, whether or not what I have said is correct, I believe that any company given recognition by the government of the day, no matter what its business may be, should be accorded subsequent privileges consistent with that recognition. This company and the company dealt with previously were granted charters. The company now under consideration, as I understand it, operated under arrangements which were then acceptable but which, if the information of the hon. member who has ju9t spoken is correct, are not now acceptable to the superintendent of insurance. Surely if our proud boast of democracy means anything, the individuals affected have the right to present their point of view. They have not the right to present those views in this house. I submit that the gentlemen who are prosecuting an endeavour in the maritime provinces, which I am sure hon. gentlemen will recognize as being a very desirable objective, should have an opportunity to come before the committee to state their views.

Why should this company which cannot obtain a licence under present arrangements come here seeking to have its privileges extended? The hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) seems to take it for granted1 that if a company has once been established' and recognized, it should go on and on.

subtopic: CENTRAL FINANCE CORPORATION
speechtext: No, I did not say that.

subtopic: CENTRAL FINANCE CORPORATION
speechtext:
Perhaps the hon. member did not say it in those words, but he implied that it should be given the privilege of having its affairs examined and of being allowed to make changes. It seems to me that if a company has not been complying with the existing regulations, there exists a very good reason why those privileges should be promptly withdrawn. Whatever may be said about the previous bill I do not think it can be said that this one is a step in the right direction.
I understand something of the reasons that may be alleged for having regulated companies. Admittedly there is something to be said for having a regulated company, even though its practices are reprehensible, but it is a desperate alternative that we are asked to adopt. If the small loan business is iniquitous, if it consists essentially in the practice of usury, why should we go on iolerating it to the extent of 24 per cent, or as in this particular case, I believe, 27 per cent per annum? Is that the alternative that we should adopt? I do not think so. There are possibilities of establishing other agencies to do this kind of work. The companies take the ground that their losses are so heavy that they have to charge this very heavy rate; that the carrying on of this business involves large expenditures and for that reason they must charge high rates. I can follow their reasoning though I cannot accept their conclusions. It may be essential for a company which goes into this business and pays its officials 86,000 a year and over in salaries, even though they charge a moderate rate of interest, say five or six per cent on their investment, to impose such rates as this in order to recoup themselves for the losses they sustain. That is all very well, looking at it

from the company's standpoint. But we in this parliament should think not so much of the company's interests as of the interests of the borrower. I submit that no man can pay around two or two and a half per cent per month and remain solvent for very long.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CENTRAL FINANCE CORPORATION
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: CENTRAL FINANCE CORPORATION
speechtext: It is that principle that we are here considering, because this bill provides for the continuance of that kind of thing. It occurs to me that the situation is very much like attempting to rescue a man who is drowning. You say, "Poor fellow, he is going down; he ought to be thrown a life preserver." But if you throw him something which is in the shape of a life preserver but which is heavier than water, you are not helping him very much; your help is simply sending him down. And if the best this house can do is to provide that private companies, regulated and all the rest of it, can charge 24 to 27 per cent interest, we are not doing very much to help out the borrowers.

subtopic: CENTRAL FINANCE CORPORATION
speechtext: Might I suggest that this is not 27 per cent per annum; it is two and a quarter per cent per month, which amounts to a great deal more than 27 per cent per annum.

subtopic: CENTRAL FINANCE CORPORATION
speechtext: Yes, I suppose that is true, although these loans are for short terms, and perhaps strictly we should not speak of them as 24 or 27 per cent per annum.

subtopic: CENTRAL FINANCE CORPORATION
speechtext: That is the difficulty. We are supposing. We don't know. Let us consider this.

subtopic: CENTRAL FINANCE CORPORATION
speechtext: But we know it is not less than 27 per cent.

subtopic: CENTRAL FINANCE CORPORATION
speechtext: The effective rate.

subtopic: CENTRAL FINANCE CORPORATION
speechtext: The effective rate is not less than 27 per cent. I do not see why, because a somewhat similar bill was passed on Friday, we should pass another bill now on .Monday. The bill that was passed on Friday was a great deal better in principle than this one.

subtopic: CENTRAL FINANCE CORPORATION
speechtext: It only slipped through.

We might, therefore, at least examine them in committee where interested parties both for and against may be heard.

Old Age Pensions

subtopic: CENTRAL FINANCE CORPORATION

subtopic: CENTRAL FINANCE CORPORATION

The house is now considering another bill -each bill standing by itself-and we are back again into the question of principle. Personally I strongly urge, and I am quite prepared to call a vote on the question, that here and now this bill should be voted down. The principle involved is that of 27 per cent interest, or much more, as the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Taylor) suggests. I think it is outrageous. In spite of the wretched conditions that prevail among a great many of the poor of this country, apparently the best thing parliament can do is to allow companies of this kind to go on exploiting, as I regard it-yes, exploiting the people. The fact that they do not exploit them to the extent of 30 or 40 per cent- someone suggested that certain companies have robbed borrowers to as much as 100 per cent, or was it 600 per cent?-that I suggest is no reason why we should permit this company to exploit people up to 27 per cent. I hope the house will vote this bill down now.

The house resumed consideration in committee of Bill No. 42, to amend the Old Age Pensions Act-Mr. Dunning-Mr. Sanderson in the chair.
On section 3-Pensions to the blind: conditions.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCLUDE CERTAIN CLASSES OF BLIND PERSONS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, section 3
(a)	of the bill, defines blindness for the purposes of the act. The definition there used is the same as is used in the Blind Persons Act of 1920 of the United Kingdom. There are many definitions of blindness, and they vary considerably-

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCLUDE CERTAIN CLASSES OF BLIND PERSONS
speechtext: There is political blindness.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCLUDE CERTAIN CLASSES OF BLIND PERSONS
speechtext:
-even in the same countries. The definitions are different, depending on whether they have reference to census enumeration, education or pensions. After careful consideration the English definition has been adopted as the most satisfactory. It is recognized that this definition is general in character, and that it will be necessary to express what it means in terms which can be used and applied by medical examiners, and section 4 of the bill provides that that may be done by regulation.
It is, however, important to note that in the definition adopted the test is not whether the person is unable to pursue his ordinary occupation or any particular occupation, but whether he is too blind to perform any work for which eyesight is essential, and that only visual conditions will be taken into account, and ether bodily or mental infirmities will be disregarded. I may amplify that by saying that in discussions with those interested in the problem, from the standpoint of the blind themselves, there is practical unanimity in expressing approval of the definition of blindness used in the British act, which has been adopted in (a) of the section now before the committee. I think it would be convenient if we adopted this section by
Old Age Pensions

alphabetical subdivisions, as (a) does not relate to (b), (c) and (d). I shall have an amendment to (c) when we reach it, but for the moment I am dealing with (a), the definition of blindness.

On paragraph (b):

Is not in receipt of a pension in respect of blindness under the pension act or an allowance in respect of blindness under the War Veterans Allowance Act.

On paragraph (d):

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCLUDE CERTAIN CLASSES OF BLIND PERSONS
speechtext: Paragraph (d) allows a total income of $440 for a blind person who is unmarried, or a widower without a child or children, or a widow without a child or children, which means that the pensioner could have a permissible income of $200 over and above the maximum pension of $240 per year. In the case of a blind person who is married, or a widower or a widow with a child or children, the maximum total income is $840 a year, and the maximum permissible income is $400 a year, or just double that for an unmarried blind person. For old age pension the maximum total income is $385 and the maximum permissible income otherwise is $125, and no distinction is made between married and unmarried persons. The extra provision here contained for blind persons recognizes, by the permissible income, a more generous scale in view of the fact that the cost of living for blind persons is higher than for seeing persons, and encourages them to support themselves and their families by augmenting their pensions by earnings. This was the subject of considerable discussion with those organizations that have to do with the blind, and I believe the committee will recognize that there is naturally a certain extra expense falling upon a blind person. There is also the further factor of the training work, work peculiarly suited to blind persons which is carried on by various institutions and which does return a certain income for the blind. For these reasons it is intended to treat blind persons more generously with respect to permissible income than the old age pensioner at seventy.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCLUDE CERTAIN CLASSES OF BLIND PERSONS
speechtext:
I do not think that any
member will suggest that we are treating the blind generously when we allow such a small earning power as this bill provides. According to the minister's statement and the terms of the bill itself, a blind single person is allowed to earn not more than $200 per year. If he earns more than that, his pension allowance is reduced accordingly. In other words, he is allowed to earn approximately $4 per week. Perhaps I might put it this way. His total maximum income, the amount he will receive as a pensioner and the amount he will be allowed to earn, will be about $8.50 a week or a little over. I do not suppose any one will claim that for a single blind person $8.50 per week can by any stretch of the imagination be called a generous amount. Would not the minister consider increasing the amount that a blind person should be allowed to earn?

Old Age Pensions
It is not a question of what he may earn, as he may have an unearned income slightly more than is provided for under this bill.
The same might be said with regard to married persons. According to the provisions of this bill the maximum income would be $640 per year, including the amount of the pension. In other words, a married person would be allowed to earn $400 per year, or a total income of a little less than $12.50 per week. I do not think anyone will say that that is treating over-liberally a blind person of the age of forty-five who may have a dependent or partly dependent family. I plead with the minister to increase the amount which a blind person may earn and still be eligible for pension. One of the great hardships under the existing old age pension legislation is that the maximum amount of income allowed a person aged seventy or over is only $365 per year. As persons become older there are times when their requirements become greater on account of sickness and invalidity, and the same thing applies to some extent to the blind pensioner. Is it asking too much, or am I not in this instance voicing the opinion of all the blind people, that they should be allowed to earn more than the amount stated in this bill?

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCLUDE CERTAIN CLASSES OF BLIND PERSONS
speechtext: I wish to add my plea to that of the last speaker. It will be remembered that in the discussion on the budget resolution I read a telegram from the blind people in Vancouver, and one of their special requests was in connection with the earning allowance for blind people.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCLUDE CERTAIN CLASSES OF BLIND PERSONS
speechtext: May I ask the minister if the persons he consulted as representing the blind were in favour of this clause in the bill?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCLUDE CERTAIN CLASSES OF BLIND PERSONS
speechtext:
I have naturally had representations from many quarters. One would expect those representing the parties who are to benefit from the bill to ask as much as possible; they would not be truly representing their people if they did not ask for enough. I may, however, tell my hon. friend that I have ample evidence that the blind people are very, very grateful indeed for the provision here made, as a start. More than that I shall not say at the moment.
To determine the relationship which shall exist in regard to income is not an easy matter. One has in mind, of course, the existing provisions of the Old Age Pensions Act. Whatever opinion there may be that the income permitted under that act should be increased, as was expressed this afternoon by many hon. members, the fact remains that the people of this dominion are putting up for the coming fiscal year $27,500,000 under that act. It is
anticipated that this additional provision will require $500,000 more during the coming year. I say to-day what I said on the introduction of the Old Age Pensions Act in 1928, that I believe this represents a very fair start, and entirely without prejudice to the future of the legislation.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCLUDE CERTAIN CLASSES OF BLIND PERSONS
speechtext:
I have not the least doubt that the blind people of this country are extremely grateful for the measure now before the committee. I have had expressions to that effect from them, but I have also had communications expressing dissent from certain provisions of this bill, and while I have had no direct communication in regard to this particular clause, I know the hardship such a provision involves for those who come under the existing Old Age Pensions Act. I know how difficult it is for old people who take in the full amount allowed and then find that they have perhaps received in pension and earnings more than they are entitled to. I know this involves a good deal of work on the part of the government, and I have no doubt they have given the matter a good deal of consideration, but I am wondering whether pensions to the blind in other countries, particularly in England or Australia, are restricted by provisions of the same kind'. I have an impression that those countries are perhaps a little more generous in their allowance for earnings than this. I am pretty sure such is the case in Australia, and I do not see why we in enacting legislation of this kind cannot be just as generous in our provisions as our sister dominions.
One question that occurs to me while I am on my feet is this: Would a blind pensioner who attains the age of seventy come under the provisions of this proposed bill or under the provisions of the existing act?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCLUDE CERTAIN CLASSES OF BLIND PERSONS
speechtext: It would not make any difference.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCLUDE CERTAIN CLASSES OF BLIND PERSONS
speechtext: It would in respect of earning capacity.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCLUDE CERTAIN CLASSES OF BLIND PERSONS
speechtext: As far as earning capacity is concerned he would come under this provision, because he is blind.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCLUDE CERTAIN CLASSES OF BLIND PERSONS
speechtext:
In speaking to this bill this afternoon I mentioned what I thought were some desirable features. I am sorry I had to leave my seat and attend the committee inquiring into the prices of farm implements and therefore did not hear the discussion after four o'clock. However, I am not coming to the rescue of the government; they do not need it. I feel more like congratulating them for establishing the principle of pensions for the blind..
Old Age Pensions

I do not think my hon. friends on the other side are entirely fair when they ask for earnings to foe permitted in excess of $200 a year, in addition to the $240 pension granted under this bill. I am more concerned about those blind persons who are not going to receive this pension, and who will receive nothing at all. I should like to make it a little easier for all blind people to receive this pension. I believe those who are entitled to come under this legislation have been taken care of, perhaps not generously, but fairly well under the circumstances.
I had a letter the other day asking me to suggest to the government that provided the applicant was a British subject, and a resident of Canada for twelve years he or she should be qualified for this pension for the blind. I do not know how the minister will receive that suggestion, but I think I would prefer that to increasing the pension, as advocated by some hon. members to the left.
Then what is going to become of blind people under the age of forty? It seems to me many of -them are in a worse position than some who have reached the age of forty, and who perhaps have acquired knowledge of some trade and are able to make a living for themselves.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCLUDE CERTAIN CLASSES OF BLIND PERSONS
speechtext: What is happening to them now?

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCLUDE CERTAIN CLASSES OF BLIND PERSONS
speechtext: I want to follow up my argument. I had a letter from a constituent who said he knew of a young man seventeen years of age, not only blind but deaf also, and he wanted to know if any provision could be made for such a person. Under this bill no such provision whatever is made. I suggest that the right to get a pension be made easier, instead of imposing too many restrictions, and I therefore urge that the age be made less than twenty years provided the person is a British subject. Put it at twelve years, as my correspondent suggests. Before increasing the amount of the pension, as some hon. gentlemen are asking, let us consider the blind under the age of forty.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCLUDE CERTAIN CLASSES OF BLIND PERSONS
speechtext:
In the discussions which I had with those interested in the blind people, representing the institutions which deal with them educationally and otherwise, one of the strongest pleas put up to the government in favour of the legislation now proposed, with the age provisions now proposed, was that if provision were made by way of pension for the blind over the age of forty, the institutions now existing for the care of the blind would be able to do very much better work in the way of education, particularly along

the lines of the vocational training of those who have not yet attained the age of forty. We are assured by those interested that the passing of this legislation will liberate the hands of these organizations and give assistance where it will do the most good, because generally speaking those who have passed the age of forty cannot readily acquire the ability to do work which will produce an income, while those under forty can be educated by the organizations interested in the welfare of the blind to enable them to earn quite reasonable sums for their own support. So I would point out to my hon. friend that the age of forty is quite acceptable to those who represent the blind in this country. I do not say they would not like a lower age, but in support of the proposal they point out that if the parliament of Canada will make provision for pensions to the blind at forty, it will enable them to do a great deal more work, and more valuable work, for those under forty than they are now able to do.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCLUDE CERTAIN CLASSES OF BLIND PERSONS
speechtext: Perhaps I should mention that I have received communications from those in charge of institutions for the blind, and they say they are very, very grateful and quite well satisfied to have these pensions apply at forty years of age.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCLUDE CERTAIN CLASSES OF BLIND PERSONS
speechtext: The age in Great Britain is fifty.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCLUDE CERTAIN CLASSES OF BLIND PERSONS
speechtext: I know those in charge of these institutions believe that now that we have established the principle of pensions for the blind we have gone a long way in taking care of these people. But I should like to ask the minister how this will affect a case such as I mentioned, that of a young man who at the age of seventeen is not only blind but also deaf. Are there any institutions that take care of cases such as that?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCLUDE CERTAIN CLASSES OF BLIND PERSONS
speechtext: I would point out to my hon. friend that normally the care of people of that kind is a provincial responsibility, and the provinces have institutions for the purpose of taking care of those who are deaf. In legislation of this kind the dominion is again taking upon its shoulders a responsibility which normally belongs to the provinces, and we are contributing seventy-five per cent of the cost of attaining that objective.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCLUDE CERTAIN CLASSES OF BLIND PERSONS
speechtext: It is a grant in aid.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCLUDE CERTAIN CLASSES OF BLIND PERSONS
speechtext:
It is a grant in aid, and I think the tendency of this parliament to deal with problems as though this parliament alone was responsible, with respect to matters which under our constitution are committed to the provinces, should be made clear. This

Old Age Pensions
is another grant in aid, and I would point out to the committee generally, not specifically to my hon. friend, that those grants in aid are creating more and more financial difficulties, not only for the dominion, but in some instances for the provinces as well. The dominion must deal with all provinces on the same basis, regardless of the ability of the individual province to meet the financial conditions laid down by the dominion. That is one of the factors, in my judgment, which require to be cleared up as between the dominion and the provinces in a constitutional sense, and it constitutes a major part of the problem which has been mentioned time and again in the house this session. Here we are definitely making a grant in aid towards meeting a provincial responsibility.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCLUDE CERTAIN CLASSES OF BLIND PERSONS
speechtext: I think perhaps one word might have been added by the minister, and it is this: When the report was made it was indicated clearly that this was not within the power of this parliament under section 91; that it came within the exclusive powers of the provinces, and that, as far as we were concerned, we could not validly legislate with respect to the matter except by a grant in aid. This is a grant in aid, and the conditions and provisions with respect to how it is to be administered must be worked out by the provinces and not by the dominion. Until there is a constitutional amendment that power will not be ours.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCLUDE CERTAIN CLASSES OF BLIND PERSONS
speechtext:
I should like to
commend the minister on having taken this step along a road which I am sure we will have to follow much further in future. Whether or not there is a constitutional difficulty in the way, this is a sound move, and I commend the minister for having made it.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCLUDE CERTAIN CLASSES OF BLIND PERSONS
speechtext:
I wish to do two things, without taking up too much time. I wish to point out to the hon. member for Portage la Prairie (Mr. Leader) that we are not criticising the government at all. Surely we can ask that the bill be enlarged or improved without being accused of criticising the government. We ask one thing; the hon. member asks another. We are not criticising the government or being unfair to it any more than the hon. member is.
I should like to support what has been urged by the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Heaps) in this connection. We are not asking that the amount of the pension be increased; we are only asking for an increase in the amount of earnings allowed before a deduction from the pension is made.
With earnings of $200 allowed in the case of an unmarried person and $400 in the case of a married person, the earning power of the blind would have to be very low before there would be any considerable increase in the amount the government would be asked to pay, even if the earnings allowed were increased considerably. We must understand that when we provide such a meagre living allowance people are continually on the border line of destitution. Consequently they cannot maintain their health; if they become ill there is no reserve, and they have no savings for an emergency. While I am quite appreciative of what the minister has been able to do, 1 wish he could see his way clear to increase the earnings allowed before any deduction is made from the pension.

The man concerned was born in Canada in August, 1866, and has resided here ever since. In the last twenty years he has resided in the following places. I place the responsibility squarely on this committee. I am going to state plainly the reason why it is proposed that when two blind persons marry, they shall receive only the pension of one.
We are extending the privileges of the old age pension to people who are over forty years of age. Some forms of blindness are congenital. Those who are interested on behalf of the blind in promoting this legislation suggest to me that it is not desirable to say to two blind people just over forty years of age, " If you two get married you can pool your pensions, blind though both of you may be."

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

But the proposal in this subsection is that if two blind people who are to-day unmarried, and who are over forty years of age, get married, they will receive not two pensions but one pension. I have attempted to state the reason. Hereditary blindness is a very difficult problem. I believe I am correct in saying that there is considerable dispute among experts with regard to the transmission of blindness from one generation to the next. But it is certain that in connection with many forms of congenital blindness the marriage of two blind persons so afflicted ensures that the children will be blind. So I am advised. If we say to two blind people, a man and a woman, that if they marry they can double up their pensions, we shall be encouraging by law that kind of marriage, and those who are interested in the welfare of the blind do not, for the most part, recommend such a provision.
The hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Taylor) quoted a telegram I had from the Vancouver branch of one of the main organizations dealing with the blind, protesting very much against what they call a discrimination. Reading the telegram, I wondered whether the sender of it imagined that the provision would apply to those who are already married. Such, as my hon. friend knows, is not the case. He thinks that I am trying to conduct an experiment in eugenics-that I believe is the term he used in his letter to me. Such is not the intention. I leave it entirely to the judgment! of this committee whether we should provide that two blind people who marry and. are suffering, fromi congenital blindness shall be enabled to double up their pensions.

The discussion so far has been confined to very few members. If I were any judge of the comments made by the committee generally, I should say that the sense of the committee was rather favourable to the section as it now stands in the bill. I am willing to listen to the discussion and, as I say, if I find a consensus of opinion along the lines indicated by my hon. friend's proposed amendment, which is out of order, I shall be pleased to deal with the matter in an orderly fashion myself. But on the basis of a snap 
Old Age Pensions
move of that sort, I cannot do so. I think we should try to treat this matter without any thought of advantage or manoeuvre or anything of that kind.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCLUDE CERTAIN CLASSES OF BLIND PERSONS
speechtext: I object to the minister using such language. If my amendment is out of order, though I claim it is not, it is not necessary for the minister to say that I am trying to get a snap decision or trying to manoeuvre. That is decidedly out of order, and should be retracted.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCLUDE CERTAIN CLASSES OF BLIND PERSONS
speechtext: I do not want to give offence to my hon. friend or anyone else. If my words have given offence to the hon. gentleman I shall be glad to withdraw them in so far as they did, and I hope he will do me the same courtesy.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCLUDE CERTAIN CLASSES OF BLIND PERSONS
speechtext: I have always tried to be as courteous as possible not only to the minister but to all other hon. members. In moving the amendment, even if it is out of order, I was only exercising my privileges in this house.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCLUDE CERTAIN CLASSES OF BLIND PERSONS
speechtext:
Apparently the committee has in a form expressed itself on this question, but I do want to bring one point before the minister, who to my mind shows a very evident intention of recognizing the difficulties that would be established by the passing of such a section. The minister knows as well as the rest of us do that propinquity is the law which will be established in this case, and that blind people already making friends of other blind people will tend to consort and to come together, and you cannot legislate against them with money or by depriving them of money. In connection with the correspondence which the minister referred to between himself and myself, if he will permit me to do so I should like to quote one excerpt:
But in this matter we develop different points of view, and if you are attempting to introduce eugenieal considerations into legislation it should not commence with the blind.
I think that point is very definite. We should not introduce into legislation for blind people matters which are better dealt with in a proper consideration of eugenics in the interest of advancing the physical condition of the people. For that reason I should very much like to see a definite expression to the effect that this paragraph should be cut out. I sincerely hope the minister will reconsider it.

I want to say a word or two before the preamble carries. I was a member of the committee that was appointed in the last house and I also supported the member for Wood Mountain (Mr. Donnelly) in this house in the projection of this legislation. I feel, therefore, that I should take this opportunity first to pay a tribute to the former member for Renfrew North, Doctor Cotnam. Although he was not a member of the committee, it was in pursuance of his resolution that the committee was appointed, and it inquired thoroughly into the whole question of pensions for the blind.
There appeared before the committee a number of witnesses who were well informed on the subject, and I think their names should be mentioned and that they should receive the compliments of the house.
I would place first Captain Baker of the Canadian National Institute for the Blind. He had made a very exhaustive study of the subject, and the evidence he gave was of great importance and assisted very much in inducing the committee to support the Cotnam resolution. Then there was Mr. Layton, of the Canadian Federation for the Blind, and a number of other witnesses whose names I do not remember.
I should like also to compliment the hon. member for Wood Mountain (Mr. Donnelly), who made an excellent speech on behalf of the blind in the house last session and well deserves the thanks of the house for the part he took in bringing this great boon to the blind.
Finanlly I want to compliment the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) because the bill could not have been introduced into the house without his consent. I am very happy that the minister was able to find the necessary money, owing perhaps to the increase in revenues, to enable him to introduce this
legislation. All hon. members are for the bill, and I am sure the whole house earnestly hopes that it will result in great relief to our unfortunate blind people.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCLUDE CERTAIN CLASSES OF BLIND PERSONS

I wish to associate myself
with what has just been said, and I hope that when the bill goes on its final journey to another chamber it will receive the same sympathetic consideration as it has here. I well remember what happened to the first old age pensions bill sent to the other chamber in 1926. I hope this time there will be a different attitude towards this measure there. This is one of the few pieces of humane legislation that we have been privileged to discuss in this house, and I am more than pleased at the unanimity of the sentiments expressed regarding it. I should also like to compliment the Minister of Finance for the thorough grasp he has shown of this question, as he does of all questions.

REGULATION OF IMPORTATION, EXPORTATION AND SALE	'
Hon. J. G. GARDINER (Minister of Agriculture) moved that the house go into committee to consider the following proposed resolution:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to control and regulate the importation, exportation, sale and other dealing with feeding stuffs by registration and inspection; the imposition of registration fees; and to authorize the Minister of Agriculture to appoint officers for the effective execution of the act.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Sanderson in the chair.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the
present Feeding Stuffs Act which the bill founded on this resolution is intended to replace has been in effect without amendment, except with regard to wheat by-products, since 1921. The purpose of this measure is to provide for the control of additional feed products; to require guarantees suited to the
different kinds of feed products now on the market; and to facilitate enforcement, and to consolidate and clarify the wording of the act where necessary or advisable.
It will be apparent to members of the committee that during the years since 1921 there have been a number of new feed stuffs for feeding animals placed upon the market, and it is intended to bring the act up to date. For the benefit of the committee I may say that when this bill is given second reading it is my intention to have it sent to a committee, in order that those interested may appear and make representations in connection with any changes that may be proposed. Therefore I would suggest that it might not be necessary to enter into any detailed discussion of the measure at this stage.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I am very seriously concerned about our power to enact legislation founded upon such a resolution, in view of the recent decisions of the court of last resort. It will be observed that we are selecting one article of commerce, namely, feeding stuffs. It will be observed that we propose to control and regulate (a) the importation, (b) the exportation and (c) the sale, and other dealings therewith. If the judgment to which I refer has any value at all it has the effect of saying that any attempt on the part of this parliament to regulate the sale would be an invalid exercise of our powers. I am not going to use technical language; I am speaking broadly and generally at the moment.
Further, these means are to be accomplished by registration and inspection. It will be recalled that the court said that it made no difference what method was used; if the purpose sought was what is sought here, then it was not a valid exercise of power by parliament to attempt to do it. The imposition of registration fees, and the authority given the minister to appoint officers and so on, are supplementary matters.
I am not going to raise the issue in any sense beyond directing attention to it at the moment. Perhaps a bill might be introduced based on this resolution, without prejudice to any position which may be taken subsequently; then the bill might be given first reading tonight and stand for second reading as soon as convenient thereafter. In the meantime I merely direct the attention of the Minister of Justice to the matter, for what it may be worth, because these words in the form in which they are now used, having regard to the language employed by the privy council, would seem to me to indicate a contemplated
Seeds

measure that would be beyond the jurisdiction of this parliament to enact. I say that regretfully, because I should like to see this parliament have that power.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I think

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Yes, against us.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Quite so.

speechtext:
As a matter of fact, since the minister has mentioned it, that is the one I am least able to understand. Had this arisen through a concrete case I say to the minister frankly that I think the judgment might have been different, because that measure provided that there should be cooperation. The minister will remember that in the Crystal Dairy case the privy council said British Columbia could not impose fees that, according to the privy council, amounted to the exercise of the taxing power in an indirect manner, which was beyond their jurisdiction. The marketing act, to which reference was made by the minister just now, certainly shared the fate of previous acts, but on the ground that in this instance it was the exercise by this parliament of powers that belonged to the province. As I say, I can hardly reconcile that. But without going into the matter at any length, I think ample opportunity to look into it will be afforded after the bill has been printed and second reading given, since the bill is to go to a committee, which appears to me to be a very proper course to pursue with respect to a matter of this kind.

Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

speakerposition: stagedirection

Hon. J. G. GARDINER (Minister of Agriculture) moved that the house go into committee to consider the following proposed resolution:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to regulate the testing, inspection, sale and importation of seeds; to provide for the appointment and definition of duties of an advisory board; the appointment of inspectors and analysts; the licensing of new varieties of seeds and the imposition of licence fees, and

to provide for penalties in consequence of violations of the act.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee. Mr. Sanderson in the chair.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
maintopic: REGULATION OF TESTING, INSPECTING, SALE AND IMPORTATION
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I think probably the comment that was made by the leader of the opposition with regard to the last bill would apply here also. The purpose of the proposed bill is to amend and consolidate the Seeds Act, in the light of the experience gained in the administration of that act and the merchandising of seeds over a period of thirteen years. The act has been on the statute books for thirteen years. We have gathered certain experience from the administration of it, and think there should be amendments to it. It is mostly a consolidation of amendments which have been made during that period of time.
I intend to make the same suggestion with regard to this measure, that it be sent to the committee on agriculture, in order that those representing seed houses and producers of seed may appear before the committee and make their representations. I would therefore suggest that the resolution be passed and that the bill based upon it be read a first time, with the understanding that the whole matter will be open for discussion at a later stage.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: REGULATION OF TESTING, INSPECTING, SALE AND IMPORTATION
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, it will be observed that there is some slight difference between the two resolutions. The resolution dealing with seeds does not purport to control. That dealing with feeding stuffs does undertake to control as well as to regulate. Of course, there has been held to be a substantial difference between the use of the words control and regulate.
The word which I believe should be given special consideration in the resolution is the word "sale." I would not go to the trouble of mentioning it now, were it not for the fact that possibly the law officers of the crown may desire to look into the matter with care. I direct the attention of the house to the word " sale " because a decision of the court of last resort apparently is to the effect that sale is a matter which is regulated by the law of the province, dealing as it does with property and civil rights. It would seem to me, indeed, difficult to indicate under what branch of section 91 of our constitution this legislative power is conferred upon the parliament of Canada. Our claim that it came within property and civil rights fails, because the court has reasserted the view that we cannot consider a specific article of trade and commerce when we are dealing with a question of regulation.

Questions
With respect to sale, I have already indicated the extreme view taken by the court in recent cases. I certainly think, however, that this parliament has complete power to deal with questions of importation. Obviously that power is exercised and has been exercised every day. But the other questions which arise are not so free from doubt.
I believe the suggested method of dealing with the measure is to be commended. The bill could - be read a first time and then after it has been given second reading-which probably would have to be without prejudice to the position which might develop after the discussion in committee as to its legality -it could be referred to the appropriate committee. Do I understand it is to be referred to a special committee or the standing committee on agriculture.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
maintopic: REGULATION OF TESTING, INSPECTING, SALE AND IMPORTATION
speechtext: The understanding is to refer them both to the standing committee on agriculture.

maintopic: REGULATION OF TESTING, INSPECTING, SALE AND IMPORTATION

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
maintopic: REGULATION OF TESTING, INSPECTING, SALE AND IMPORTATION
speechtext:
Speaking offhand I
believe it is now by the minister, but I would not be certain.

maintopic: REGULATION OF TESTING, INSPECTING, SALE AND IMPORTATION
speechtext: I do not think so.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
maintopic: REGULATION OF TESTING, INSPECTING, SALE AND IMPORTATION
speechtext: That is a matter which can be discussed.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: REGULATION OF TESTING, INSPECTING, SALE AND IMPORTATION
speechtext:
It depends on the grade of the office. Some of the -day-to-day men and field men are appointed by the minister; others are appointed by the civil service commission.
